description: We are CrewSentiq, two Computer Science students building practical technology for human space exploration. Our project is an astronaut-focused health dashboard that turns simulated vital signs, sleep, and activity data into clear trends and early alerts. We enjoy full-stack development, data visualization, and AI-assisted problem solving. We welcome teammates with UI/UX, health research, or data engineering skills who want to build an intuitive mission-support prototype.
summary:
CrewSentiq is an offline-first crew health monitoring platform for long-duration space missions. We built a working web app that compares every crew member only against their own baseline, using a sustained 15% change rule and a robust z-score, built on NASA’s Human Research Program hazard and risk data. It maps results onto 11 NASA-linked conditions and shows the computed severity stage on an interactive human digital twin, with the possible outcomes and NASA reference text.

It addresses the challenge by giving a crew early, explainable health awareness without internet or a ground link. It also protects privacy: administrators see all crew, while each crew member sees only their own data.

This matters because on missions far from Earth, radiation, isolation and altered gravity change each person’s body slowly, and help may be minutes away. The platform runs from one command, uses simulated data (clearly labelled), and has 24 passing automated tests.

This is about 150 words, inside the 50-200 range. If the challenge page uses specific wording, tell me and I’ll mirror it.
details:
What it does and how it works

CrewSentiq monitors crew health on long missions and checks each person only against their own history. It stores nine metrics per crew member: heart rate, sleep, activity, hydration, body temperature, radiation dose, cabin CO2, mood and workload. It sets each person’s baseline from their earlier readings.

  • Alerts: it raises a review alert when a metric stays at least 15% off baseline for 3 consecutive readings. It raises a watch alert when the robust z-score, Z = (X - median) / (1.4826 x MAD), reaches |Z| of 3 or more.
  • Condition Atlas: it maps results onto 11 conditions linked to NASA risk modules. Each has five severity stages, a spectrum of states, possible outcomes and NASA reference text.
  • Digital twin: the affected organs light up on an interactive human body.
  • Access: an administrator sees all crew, and a crew account sees only its own data. The server enforces this.

Benefits

  • It works with no internet, cloud or database server, and starts with one command.
  • It judges each person against themselves, which avoids false alarms from population averages.
  • Every alert shows its evidence, formula and NASA source, so it is explainable.
  • It protects each crew member’s data from the others.
  • It includes a filter engine, CSV export and a NASA reference library.

Intended impact

We want crews and mission operators to notice slow, individual health changes early, even when the link to Earth is delayed. Our longer-term aim is a transparent, open tool that analog habitats, research programmes and commercial missions could adopt, and that isolated-work settings on Earth could use too. Real impact would need real sensor data and clinical validation, which we have not done yet.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SVG
  • Backend: FastAPI and uvicorn
  • Database: local JSON files
  • Frontend: vanilla JavaScript with hand-built SVG charts, no build tools
  • Testing: pytest (24 tests, all passing)
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop or desktop; no special sensors for the demo
  • Software: Python 3.9 or newer and a web browser
  • Data: NASA Human Research Program hazard, risk and metric datasets

How it is creative

  • Within-person approach: it asks “is this normal for THEM?” instead of using population ranges.
  • Digital twin: it turns slow numerical drift into a visible picture of the affected organs and stage, which a non-specialist can follow.
  • Spectrum view: it shows the whole range from baseline to a possible medical event, not just a single alert.
  • Single-folder design: one process serves the whole app and plain JSON files act as the database, which makes it unusually simple to install and inspect.

Factors our team considered

  • Offline use: deep-space links are slow or absent.
  • Privacy: access control is enforced on the server, not just hidden in the interface.
  • Data honesty: all measurements are simulated and labelled as such, since NASA files describe what to measure and contain no real crew records.
  • Safety: thresholds are screening aids, not clinical cut-offs, and the app says it does not diagnose.
  • Explainability: every alert traces back to its readings and rule.
  • Reviewer experience: judges can install, run and test it in minutes without a team present.
  • Honest scope: three conditions are reference-only because no sensor feed exists, and the next steps are real sensor adapters, a SQL database, TLS and clinical validation.
